title: Protocol for single-molecule labeling and tracking of bacterial cell division proteins
protocol: Streak cells from a frozen stock onto fresh LB plates with the appropriate antibiotics.
Incubate the plates at 30°C or 37°C for 15–24 h.
Pick up several single colonies from the LB plates using inoculating loops or pipette tips.
Inoculate picked colonies into separate tubes containing 3 mL of growth medium.
Allow cells to grow with shaking at 220 rpm at 25°C for ∼15 h (in M9) or ∼5 h (in EZRDM).
Measure the OD600 of cultures to check their growth stages.
If the OD600 is between 0.1 and 0.3, proceed to step 2 (POI-HaloTag) or step 4 (POI-FP).
If the OD600 is higher than 0.3, re-inoculate a small portion of the culture into fresh growth medium.
Monitor the OD600 every 30 minutes or one hour until it reaches 0.1 to 0.3.
Aspirate 1 mL of cell culture from step 1c into a 1.5 mL EP tube.
Add 0.1–10 μL of 1 μM JF646 (or JFX650) Halo ligand to the culture for final concentration of 0.1–10 nM.
Vortex the culture gently for a few seconds to ensure thorough mixing.
Adjust the ligand concentration according to labeling results to achieve one or two molecules per cell for effective single-molecule tracking.
Cover the tube with alumina foil.
Incubate the cells for 30 min at 25°C with gentle rocking.
Wash the cells three times using 1 mL or 500 μL of the imaging medium or buffer.
Incubate the cells at 25°C for 5 min with gentle rocking during each wash.
Pellet the cells with a bench-top spinner or centrifuge at ∼8000 g for 2 min.
Resuspend the cell pellet from the final wash in ∼50 μL fresh culture medium (M9 or EZRDM) or other fresh media used for cell growth for imaging.
Measure and adjust the OD600 of the final culture to fall within the range of 1–3.
Gently mix ∼10 mg of SeaPlaque GTG low melting temperature Agarose in ∼500 μL of M9 or EZRDM to achieve a final concentration of 2% (W/V).
Heat the mixture at 70°C in a metal heat block or water bath for half an hour.
Place the microaqueduct slide with a 0.75-mm thick gasket on the benchtop.
Apply 50–100 μL of melted agarose gel to the center of the slide.
Cover the droplet of gel immediately with a pre-cleaned cover glass.
Allow the gel to solidify at 25°C for at least 30 min.
Store the prepared gel pad in a humidified box near the microscope if imaging will occur later.
Start imaging 20–30 min after assembling and settling the sample on the microscope.
Apply 0.5–1 μL of cell culture onto the top of the solidified gel pad.
Wait 2–3 min, then cover it with a new clean dry glass.
Assemble the FCS chamber according to the manufacturer’s instructions.
Securely position the sample chamber on the microscope stage.
Visualize cells in bright-field mode to ensure they are appropriately settled on the gel pad and display the expected morphology.
Stop the single-molecule tracking experiment if cells exhibit abnormal morphologies.
Proceed with the imaging experiment only when cell growth and division occur as predicted phenotypes.
Ensure that cells do not move or drift on the gel pad.
Search around the gel pad to find a field of view where cells remain still.
Prepare a new gel pad by carefully adjusting conditions such as the size of the gel pad and drying time for the topped cell culture if necessary.
Adjust the time after applying the cell culture based on environmental temperature and humidity.
Measure the laser power and calculate the power density.
Switch the illumination mode to Epi, which allows the laser beam to pass through the sample perpendicularly.
Set the laser output power to a range of 10–100 mW.
Measure the laser power at the top of the sample.
Capture a snapshot of the sample, identifying the illumination region as the portion with high background.
Calculate the power density by dividing the laser power by the area of the illumination region.
Adjust the excitation power density by tuning the laser output or adding a neutral density filter (DNF1) in the excitation optical path.
Measure and adjust the excitation power density to achieve a good signal-to-noise ratio for single-molecule detection and localization.
Avoid rapid photobleaching during adjustment of the excitation power density.
Increase the laser power if molecules move faster, requiring shorter exposure times.
Take streaming SMT movies.
Switch the illumination to HILO mode by laterally moving the stage until the incident angle of the laser beam reaches 60°–70°.
Focus at approximately 200 nm above the bottom of cells (about a quarter of an E. coli cell or half of a C. crescentus cell).
Capture images continuously with an exposure time of 0.5–1 s for 3–5 min.
Take bright-field images before and after fluorescence imaging to compare cell positions.
Exclude cells showing apparent movement or drifting from further data processing steps.
Perform Z-position calibration for 3D-SMT by imaging 1:500 diluted TetraSpeck fluorescent microspheres with an average diameter of 0.1 μm.
Capture 100 Z-stacks around the spheres with a step size of 20 nm.
Focus near the cell's bottom (or top) for E. coli cells to obtain more trajectories in the lateral X-Y plane.
For C. crescentus, focus on the mid-cell to monitor all molecules across the septum.
Use a longer exposure time or slower frame rate to track slowly moving molecules and filter out rapidly diffusing ones along the cylindrical part of the cell body.
Detect single-molecule signals in each frame.
Determine the central position of each molecule accurately.
Generate coordinates for molecules to be used in subsequent steps.
Localize each molecule with high spatial resolution in 2D or 3D.
Prepare directories on the computer for batch-processing using ThunderSTORM.
Create a separate folder to store all the single-molecule images (.tif files) from experiments conducted under the same conditions.
Create another folder to save the resulting localization lists.
Generate the calibration curve using the Z-stack images of the TetraSpeck fluorescent microspheres.
In the ImageJ menu, click Plugin>Macros>Install.
Select the modified macro file.
Click the button with the name of the macro file appearing at the bottom of the Plugin>Macros menu.
Select the folder containing .tif files.
Select a second folder to save results as .csv files.
Note: The process may take several hours depending on data size and computer speed.
Launch MATLAB.
Change the current directory to the folder containing all the result .csv files from step 12.
Run spotsLinking.m.
Set the Spatial Threshold to ∼300 nm.
Set the Time Threshold to a large value (i.e., 30 or 50 frames).
Set the Time Threshold to characterize the off-time distribution under current imaging conditions.
Adjust the Weight of Z to 0 for 2D imaging or to 1 for 3D imaging according to experimental setup.
Load Coordinate files and select all .csv files for analysis.
Readjust the Time Threshold based on calculated average off-time.
Set the Minimal Trace length to an appropriate value, which determines shortest trajectory length.
Click Link the spots and Save file.
Use current parameters to process all loaded files.
Save linked trajectories from each file in a new file.
Run TraceRefine.m in MATLAB.
A new GUI will appear for interactive removal of “bad trajectories”.
Change Pixel Size according to microscope setting.
Load BF/FL image by clicking Load BF/FL image.
Load trace by clicking Load trace.
Load the bright-field image and its corresponding trajectory file from step 19.
Adjust intensity thresholds by dragging the Max and Min bars.
Remove all too bright or dim molecules by clicking Intensity Refine.
Select regions of interest (ROI) using polygons to enclose trajectories.
Save chosen trajectories by clicking Save Selected Traces.
Optionally save the current GUI interface by clicking Save image.
Run RegionCrop_unwrap.m to initiate a new GUI.
Adjust the PixelSize if necessary.
Enter the date of the experiment or data processing to replace the YYYYMMDD at the top of the GUI.
Click Load BF and Load Traj to input the bright-field image and its trajectory file from step 26.
Select ROI in the GUI.
Crop a rectangular region around a specific cell’s top-left and bottom-right corners, ensuring it encompasses an entire cell with surrounding empty spaces.
Display chosen cell and its associated trajectories in a new window.
Rotate image by inputting an angle in degrees to align the cell's long axis vertically.
Click Select Center on the bright-field image to accurately select the center of the septum.
Generate Unwrap Coords.
Click on the cross points of the red scanline and the left plateau first, followed by the cross point on the right side.
The GUI will mark the selected cross points on the line and also on the bright-field image.
Repeat this step if the selection appears unsatisfactory.
Click Save the Structure.
Run RegionCrop_unwrap3D.m to initiate a new GUI.
Adjust the PixelSize if necessary.
Enter the date of the experiment or data processing to replace the YYYYMMDD at the top of the GUI.
Click Load BF and Load Traj to input the bright-field image and its filtered trajectory file from step 24.
The trajectories will be superimposed on the bright-field image, each displayed in a distinct color.
Click Select ROI.
Crop a rectangular ROI by clicking on a specific cell’s top-left and bottom-right corners.
Ensure the ROI encompasses an entire cell in the center with surrounding empty spaces of approximately 1–2 cells.
Rotate Image and input an angle in degrees to align the cell’s long axis vertically.
Select Center of Ring and click on the center of the septum on the bright-field image accurately.
Generate Ring Diameter by clicking on the cross points of the red scanline with the left plateau first, followed by the right side.
Select Center of Cell and then click on the center of the non-constricted cell cylinder on the bright-field image accurately.
Choose Left Side Region and Choose Right Side Region are tools for calculating the bright-field image's left- and right-side plateau.
Click Generate Cell Diameter.
Click on the cross points of the red scanline and the left plateau first, followed by the cross point on the right side.
The GUI will mark the selected cross points on the line and the bright-field image (in yellow and black lines).
Repeat this step if the selection appears unsatisfactory.
Click Save the Structure, and the data will be saved, returning the GUI to its main interface.
Click Save Data to auto-save all the rotated trajectories with the cropped bright-field images in the data structure.
Click Delete all to clear the workspace before processing the next file.
Generate a simulated set of stationary trajectories with varying lengths using Section 0 of the statesSegP.m file.
Fit a segment of a trajectory's position against time using a linear function.
Calculate the overall displacement from the fit.
Assess whether the displacement exceeds random fluctuations attributable to diffusion and localization uncertainty.
Simulate a set of confined diffusion segments to establish the displacement distribution for stationary molecules.
Calculate the MSD curves in the X-axis for all trajectories.
Calculate the MSD curves in the Y-axis for all trajectories.
Set the noise level of X similar to or ∼ 10%–20% larger than the first point of the MSD in the X-axis.
Set the confinement of Y similar to the plateau of the MSD in the Y-axis or the known Z-ring width.
Save the refined and combined data structure.
Confirm that Input_Params.ExpT and Input_Params.PixelS are correct according to the exposure time and pixel size used in the experiment.
Ensure Input_Params.TimeRange covers the maximum length of the trajectories.
Select the experimental dataset from step 43 and the simulation dataset from step 42 in the pop-up window.
Generate a new variable called IndTrack containing all trajectory information.
Change the Index value from 1 to the length of IndTrack.
Run Section 3 of statesSegP.m for each trajectory.
For each trajectory, a GUI will appear displaying the bright-field image with a color-coded trajectory.
Select one part of the trajectory located on the septum by clicking Okay in the pop-up box and then clicking on the two ends of the region you want to choose.
If the entire trajectory is correctly localized in the septal region, click Useall for automatic calculation.
If the trajectory is not in the area of interest (out of the septum), click Bad Trajectory to exit and continue analyzing the next one.
Examine the trajectory along the short axis displayed in the upper right region by eye.
Approximately pinpoint intervals characterized by a consistent speed or uniform slope.
Open the DwellSpeedCalc.m file.
Adjust the segmentation parameters.
Run the code.
Set Rmax1 to 0.5.
Set Pmin to 0.75.
Set Rmax2 to 0.2 if necessary for improved classification accuracy.
Select segments classified from step 46.
Save variables containing apparent moving speed and lifetime of each segment.
Plot the classification result (R and P scattered plot).
Plot the speed distribution in logarithmic scale.
Plot dwell time distribution for both stationary and moving states.
Save all plots and results.
Perform non-linear fitting of the speed distribution.
Fit the cumulative probability density function (CDF) of the speed to a single or double log-normal distribution using cdfFitting2pop.m.
Calculate the CDF of the directional speed in Section 2 of the code.
Estimate the standard errors of the fitting parameters by bootstrapping in Section 3.
Generate the histogram in the log scale of the experimental data and fitting curves in Section 4.
Calculate and fit MSD curves using MSDCalc.m to obtain diffusion and confinement information.
Extract more information from single-molecule trajectories using customized data analysis tools.
